summary: Guidance for designers of key management protocols that work with Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting systems. It stresses that designing secure, long-lasting key management is hard, and that groups without deep expertise should not invent their own. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Making secret-key handshakes is very tricky. This is advice for builders so they do not accidentally make a weak one.

subtitle: Rules of thumb for anyone designing the key handoff between a login server, a network device and a user.

tldr.problem: Networks often use a central AAA server to authenticate users and then hand keys to access devices that cannot easily make their own. Key management protocols are subtle, and ad hoc designs have poorly understood security properties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements (MUST) and recommendations (SHOULD) that any AAA key management proposal has to meet, such as algorithm independence, fresh session keys, limited key scope, replay protection and unique key names.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 132) that applies to documents requesting publication as IETF RFCs. Its authors call the requirements the Housley Criteria.

today: RFC 4962 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 132). According to the metadata on this site it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: What the Guidance Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4962 gives architectural guidance to designers of AAA key management protocols. AAA stands for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting. AAA key management is usually a collection of protocols: the AAA protocol itself, plus other protocols that handle authentication and set up security associations.

The central warning is that designing secure, long-lasting key management is hard even for experts. The RFC says it is almost certainly inappropriate for IETF working groups without deep expertise in the area to design their own key management algorithms and protocols on top of AAA. The guidance also targets other standards bodies that build on EAP, RADIUS and Diameter.

Most of the requirements come from a March 2003 presentation by Russ Housley to the AAA Working Group at IETF 56, and over the next years the set became known as the Housley Criteria.
sections.eli5: Making a secret-key system is like designing a lock. Even clever people miss mistakes, so this RFC says: do not invent your own unless you really know how.

sections.title: How Compliance Is Judged
sections.content:
The RFC uses the keywords of RFC 2119. A proposal that fails even one MUST or MUST NOT statement is not compliant. A proposal that meets every MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and SHOULD NOT statement is unconditionally compliant. One that meets all the MUST and MUST NOT statements but not every SHOULD is conditionally compliant.

The guidance is mandatory to implement but not mandatory to use. A particular deployment may be configured so that it does not follow every requirement. The RFC's example is Diameter: key confidentiality is mandatory to implement there, because EAP keying material can be delivered from a AAA server to a AAA client without disclosure to third parties, but it is not mandatory to use.
sections.eli5: It is like a school rulebook with must-do and should-do items. Break a must-do and you fail. Skip only some should-dos and you still pass, but with a lower grade.

sections.title: Why Key Management Is Easy to Get Wrong
sections.content:
The RFC opens with history. The first key management protocol in the open literature appeared in 1978. A flaw and a fix were published in 1981, the fix was broken in 1994, and in 1995 a new flaw was found in an area the earlier problems did not touch. The RFC notes that all of these flaws were obvious once described, yet no one had spotted them. The lesson: experts miss problems, so review by multiple experts is essential, and formal methods can help.

It then makes the case for algorithm independence. DES was well designed, but its 56-bit key size was eventually overcome by Moore's Law. Flaws have also been found in CHAP, MS-CHAPv1, MS-CHAPv2, Kerberos and LEAP. RADIUS mandates MD5 for integrity protection, which has known deficiencies, and has no way to negotiate a replacement.

The other principle is least privilege: each party gets only the privileges, and only the keys, needed for its role. In EAP, the peer and the server are the only parties allowed to hold all the keying material; the authenticator gets only what its role needs.
sections.eli5: People keep finding holes in secret-code systems years after they were thought safe. So build the system so a broken piece can be swapped out, and give each helper only the keys they truly need.

sections.title: The Core Requirements
sections.content:
The goal of AAA key management is to provide keying material when the peer and authenticator cannot derive keys themselves, for example because the authenticator lacks computing power or resources, or because it is undesirable for each authenticator to run its own key management conversation. Acceptable solutions MUST meet all the requirements in Section 3. The main ones are:

  • Cryptographic algorithm independent. The protocol MUST support negotiating algorithms, with at least one mandatory-to-implement suite. An EAP method MAY depend on one algorithm. Without IPsec protection, RADIUS does not meet this because its integrity algorithm cannot be negotiated.
  • Strong, fresh session keys. Each session gets an independent key, even if EAP keying material is cached. Session keys MUST NOT depend on one another, so disclosing one does not help find another.
  • Replay detection. AAA, EAP and secure association exchanges MUST be replay protected.
  • Keying material confidentiality and integrity. These MUST be maintained.
  • Confirm ciphersuite selection. The choice SHOULD be securely confirmed and roll-back attacks SHOULD be detected.

Fresh keys are required even when a long replay counter that "will never wrap" is used.
sections.eli5: Every visit should get a brand new key, like a fresh padlock for each trip. The locks must not be linked, and you should be able to swap the lock design if someone finds a weakness.

sections.title: Scope, Names and Context for Keys
sections.content:
Several requirements are about knowing exactly who holds which key.

  • Limit key scope. Following least privilege, parties MUST NOT have keying material they do not need. A protocol that sets up session keys MUST say to which parties the key is available.
  • Uniquely named keys. All keys MUST be uniquely named, and a key name MUST NOT directly or indirectly disclose the keying material. The RFC reasons that "objects that cannot be named cannot be managed".
  • Prevent the domino effect. Compromising one peer MUST NOT expose keys held by another peer, and compromising one authenticator MUST NOT expose another's. In a key hierarchy, a compromise in one branch MUST NOT compromise other branches. Group keys are the stated exception.
  • Bind key to its context. Keying material MUST be bound to how it will be used, who else has access, and its expected lifetime. A child key's lifetime SHOULD NOT be longer than its parent's.

All parties with legitimate access to a key MUST share the same context for it, which requires that they are properly identified and authenticated.
sections.eli5: Give every key its own name tag that does not give away the key. Keep each helper's keys separate so that if one helper loses theirs, everyone else's still work.

sections.title: Authenticating and Authorizing Parties
sections.content:
Each party in the protocol MUST be authenticated to the parties it talks to, and authentication mechanisms MUST NOT use plaintext passwords. Passwords are allowed only if they are never sent to another party without confidentiality protection.

Authorization is a separate step. Peer and authenticator authorization MUST be performed, and each MUST show possession of the right keying material without disclosing it. It is REQUIRED whenever a peer associates with a new authenticator. The RFC points out that proof of possession is not proof of authorization: in IEEE 802.11i, the 4-way handshake shows that peer and authenticator hold the same EAP keying material, but not that the backend server authorized the authenticator to hold it. Where AAA proxies exist, one authenticator could impersonate another unless each link checks against it. Channel binding lets the peer check that the authenticator's identity claim is consistent.

Section 4 adds two SHOULD-level recommendations. EAP methods are encouraged to protect the peer's identity, though that is not a requirement. If a peer's authorization is restricted, for example by key lifetime, SSID, Called-Station-ID or Calling-Station-ID, the peer SHOULD be told.
sections.eli5: Proving you know the secret handshake is not the same as being allowed in. The club must also check its guest list, and if you have limits, such as only until 5 o'clock, it should tell you.

sections.title: Trust in the AAA Server and Authenticator
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is about who is trusted. The AAA server is trusted to give the authenticator only the keying material it established with the peer, and to give it to no one else. In many systems the server could derive other keys from secrets it holds, and it is trusted not to. The authenticator is trusted not to pass on the keying material it receives, and any keys it derives go only to the appropriate party known to the peer.

The EAP authenticator and AAA client are expected to be on the same entity. Then one authenticator identity goes both to the AAA server and to the EAP peer, which lets them confirm the authenticator is consistent and avoids impersonation. If they are not colocated, key scope is not synchronized, which opens vulnerabilities including impersonation. The design must keep key scope and key naming unambiguous.

For management, MIB modules for AAA protocols or EAP methods MUST NOT include objects for private keys or symmetric keys. They MAY expose key names and context, and MAY allow keys to be deleted.
sections.eli5: The helpers in the middle must be trusted to carry the note without peeking or copying it. Make sure any tool that lists keys shows only their names, never the secrets.

sections.title: Appendix: How AAA Key Management Grew
sections.content:
The appendix tells the history. AAA began with Network Access Servers (NASes). TACACS was designed by BBN for the Terminal Access Controller in the ARPAnet. As PPP dial-in grew, keeping user lists on each NAS stopped scaling, so central AAA servers appeared in RADIUS and Diameter.

PAP and CHAP only authenticate the PPP peer to the NAS. PAP sends a cleartext password and is deprecated; CHAP is MD5 based but not mutual and is vulnerable to dictionary attack. MS-CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 added mutual authentication and key derivation, but flaws were found in them too. Fixing any of these meant deploying new code on both PPP peers and the AAA server, which led to EAP and its pass-through mode. Only the EAP peer and AAA server need new code to adopt a method. Vendor-specific RADIUS attributes carried keys from the server to the NAS, and a vulnerability was later found in that key wrap technique.

Pure two-party schemes are rarely deployed, since a central server eases certificate deployment and is needed for authorization and accounting. IKEv2 supports EAP methods, so carrying EAP-derived keys within AAA is required where the EAP method derives keys.
sections.eli5: Each time a password trick turned out to be weak, replacing it meant updating every device. EAP was invented so only the two ends need updating while the helpers in the middle just pass things along.
